cells.tense: You are inside the turning now, and the practice catches each arrival cleanly.
cells.act: close the cycle and leave the door open for the next
cells.ask: Finish one stretch of the practice — the run of sessions, the piece you've been refining — and leave what follows it undecided on purpose.
cells.core:
Something is arriving, and the practice is where you meet it. Not waiting for it, not rehearsing it — the repetitions are the meeting. That's why the work feels level instead of charged: you're not chasing a state, you're at the door when the knock comes, and the hands already know the door.

This is a good place to be, and it has one edge worth watching. A practice that meets arrival perfectly can also extend a cycle past its natural close, because finishing feels like stopping. So end one stretch and don't plan what follows it. Let the run of sessions finish, the piece you've been refining reach its last step — and leave the next beginning undecided. The open door is what keeps you at the door. What opens next doesn't need your calendar.
cells.sheetLine: You're at the door, and the practice is how you're there.
cells.place: at the small, steady work that gets kept

cells.tense: The current is pulling you beyond the practice, and you'll be somewhere else by the time you arrive.
cells.act: gather what it became and set it down whole
cells.ask: Bring what the practice has already made to its close — mark the end, and add nothing further to it.
cells.core:
You're being carried, and the practice has stopped being where you meet things — it's where you're already past them. Tomorrow's version of the work gets planned while today's reps run, and the sessions get looser as the vision gets brighter. There's nothing wrong with the vision. It's just running past your hands, so arrivals no longer land; they're old news by the time they happen.

What pulls you back is finishing something. Take what the practice already made — a piece, a run of sessions, a skill it built — and bring it to a close: mark the end and add nothing more. Not abandoning the practice; closing one loop inside it. A finished thing puts you back in the same moment as your hands, which is the only place arrival can happen. You'll feel the pulling stop for a minute. That's the point.

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door the practice has already walked you through.
cells.act: let the finished thing be the start of something
cells.ask: Take one skill the practice already made and start its next thing from it — one small session, on the calendar.
cells.core:
The practice is still there. The hands keep the schedule. What's missing is any sense that something is arriving — the repetitions run and nothing meets them. Somewhere along the way the work got treated as finished, or the idea of arrival got set aside as something that happens to other people, and the effort has been running thin since.

Don't push effort or feeling back into the sessions; that's how this stays stuck. Charge the other end instead. Take one thing the practice already made — a skill, a piece, a page — and use it as the start of something rather than the end of one. One first session of the next thing, small, on the calendar. You're not being asked to want it. The want returns through the doing, which is how it has worked here. The next thing is already there. The calendar is the door.

cells.tense: The pen is down, and the practice is writing without you noticing you wrote it.
cells.act: choose this, not that, and mean it
cells.ask: Take the practice exactly as it stands right now, decide to keep it or drop it, and hold that this week.
cells.core:
You talk about the practice like it has its own momentum — it's going well, it's gone quiet, sessions are happening. But the shape of it is a series of decisions you've been making, and the deciding hasn't been part of the picture. That's why the same patterns come back and surprise you: they were decided, and you weren't present when it happened. You don't know you're doing it. You're doing it.

So make one of those decisions visible. Look at the practice as it stands — building a skill, holding a routine, avoiding a piece you keep circling — then keep it or drop it, and hold that this week. Not forever. A practice you chose deliberately is yours to keep or put down; one you drift through keeps happening to you. That difference is the whole of it.
cells.sheetLine: The practice is deciding, and you've been calling it momentum.
cells.place: at the small, steady work that gets kept

attempts.check: The one unsupported claim is that the person's practice has become a cycle they can't see the seams of — the record supports 'unconscious patterns cycling' and 'surprise at obvious consequences', but nothing about what they built, how long, or what it cost them. A reader could reasonably say 'I know exactly what I'm doing, I'm just tired of it' — which is a different thing, and the Disowned cell is written so that answer is still useful: the ask is to name the thing and stand in it, which works whether they're asleep at the wheel or awake and steering. The ask survives being wrong because it asks for a choice made out loud, not a diagnosis accepted. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person: 'You recognize yourself as the turning' — it's the record's own face and it's flattering; I've kept it out of the core and left it implicit in the practice, not asserted about them.
